questions.q: Why can Silver no longer be fully rewritten every night now that Bronze ingestion is incremental?
options: Because Bronze now only holds new rows, and fully rebuilding Silver from everything would waste work reprocessing rows that haven't changed
Because Delta Lake tables can only be written to once per day
Because `silver.sales_clean` no longer has a schema
Because PySpark cannot read a Delta table more than once
questions.explain: A full rewrite made sense when Bronze was small enough to fully reprocess; now it's wasteful, so Silver needs a real upsert instead.

questions.q: In `MERGE INTO silver.sales_clean AS target USING bronze_incremental AS source ON ... WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *`, what does the `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *` branch do?
options: If an incoming row's transaction_id has no match in silver.sales_clean, insert it as a new row
Deletes any row in silver.sales_clean that wasn't in today's batch
Updates every existing row in silver.sales_clean regardless of match
Skips the row entirely and logs an error
questions.explain: WHEN NOT MATCHED means the source row's transaction_id wasn't found in the target table, so it's a brand-new transaction and gets inserted.

questions.q: Why is `transaction_id` the correct match key for the MERGE, rather than `store_id`?
options: Because store_id identifies a store, not a single sale — many different transactions share the same store_id, so matching on it would treat unrelated sales as the same row
Because store_id is not stored as an integer
Because transaction_id is always smaller in value than store_id
Because Delta Lake's MERGE INTO syntax requires the match key to start with the letter t
questions.explain: A MERGE match key must uniquely identify one logical record. store_id identifies a store shared by many transactions, so it would cause incorrect overwrites or collapsed rows.

questions.q: What is `bronze_incremental` in the MERGE statement's USING clause?
options: Only today's new incoming Bronze rows, not the full bronze.sales_raw table
The entire bronze.sales_raw table, every row ever ingested
A copy of gold.daily_sales_summary
The watermark table meta.last_ingested_date
questions.explain: The MERGE is deliberately scoped to just the incremental batch picked up by today's ingestion run, not the whole Bronze table.

questions.q: What would go wrong if the MERGE matched on sale_date instead of transaction_id?
options: Every transaction from the same store on the same day would be treated as the same row, collapsing many distinct sales into one
Nothing — sale_date and transaction_id behave identically for this table
The MERGE statement would fail to compile
It would only affect rows ingested before the watermark table existed
questions.explain: sale_date identifies a day, not a single sale; a single store can have thousands of transactions on one day, so matching on it would silently collapse distinct rows together.
